newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Lawyers' group readies for Rwanda genocide appeal.
newsitem.headline: Lawyers' group readies for Rwanda genocide appeal.

text.p: A first group of lawyers from an international justice group leaves for Rwanda this week to help in the trials of thousands of Hutus charged with crimes of genocide.
Jean Flamme, secretary general of Avocats sans Frontieres (Lawyers without Borders) said on Tuesday three lawyers would arrive in Kigali on Saturday to open a permanent office in the Rwandan capital.
"Our mission is going ahead," Flamme said. "Our project "Justice for all in Rwanda' begins in earnest this weekend."

Flamme said the team's first mission would be to see what assistance they can give to two Hutus sentenced to death last week for their role in the 1994 genocide of up to one million Tutsis and moderate Hutus.
Deogratias Bizimana, a former medical assistant, and Egide Gatanazi, a former administrator, were sentenced to death on January 3 in the southeastern town of Kibungo.
They were found guilty after a four-hour trial on December 27 during which neither man was represented by defence lawyers. They have been given until January 18 to appeal.
The pair were the first of an estimated 90,000 Rwandans crammed into jails across the country and charged with genocide crimes.
Human rights groups have welcomed the start of the trials but pointed out that the accused lacked defence representation.
"We first want to see what help, if any, we can offer these two," said Flamme. "Apart from this specific case we have a lot more work to get involved in."
The lawyers -- Macha Sinegre from France, Paul Atita from Benin and Patricia Jaspris from Belgium -- would be based in Rwanda for up to a year, Flamme said.
"If the work becomes more pressing we will send more lawyers," Flamme said. "It all depends on the need."
Rwanda's judicial system was left in ruins following the genocide, which finally ended when the Tutsi-dominated Rwandan Patriotic Front overthrew the former Hutu government.
Lawyers, prosecutors, magistrates and judges were either key targets of the genocide or fled the country to escape responsibility for their role.
Many of the suspected masterminds of the genocide are believed to be living in Africa, Europe or the United States.
An international tribunal on the Rwandan genocide opened its first trials at its headquarters in Arusha, Tanzania in 1996, but it cannot impose the death penalty on those found guilty.
"We are not going to Rwanda just to defend those on genocide charges," said Flamme. "We are also going to help the Rwandan authorities in prosecuting criminals and establishing a judicial system."
Flamme said his organisation -- established in Belgium in 1991 -- had received "every assistance" from Rwandan authorities and he was confident the group could make a positive contribution.
